```{r setup}
library(softcats)
```

## The problem

Suppose we want the difference in an outcome between groups, but the group
of each observation is not recorded. A classifier trained on a small labelled
sample gives, for every observation, the probability of belonging to each
group. The common next step is to assign each observation its most likely
group, or the group whose probability passes a confidence threshold, and to
run a regression on these labels.

That step loses information. Observations whose probabilities are close to
each other receive different labels, and uncertain observations are treated
as certain. The estimated group difference is distorted (for two groups,
typically attenuated), and its confidence interval can miss the true value far
more often than the nominal level allows.

softcats keeps the categories soft: it estimates the group difference from
the probabilities themselves.

## A first example

`sim_softcats()` simulates data in which the probabilities are calibrated,
the true effects are known and a labelled subsample is flagged. Here there
are three groups, `A` (the reference), `B` and `C`, three controls and an
outcome `y`.

```{r data}
d <- sim_softcats(n = 3000, K = 3, seed = 1)
head(d[, c("y", "x1", "x2", "x3", "prob_A", "prob_B", "prob_C")])
attr(d, "tau")
```

`soft_lm()` takes a formula with the outcome and the controls, and the class
probabilities. The probabilities can be given as column names, a one-sided
formula, a matrix, or, for two groups, a single vector.

```{r fit}
fit <- soft_lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, probs = c("prob_A", "prob_B", "prob_C"),
               data = d, learner = lrn_lm(degree = 3), seed = 1)
summary(fit)
```

The coefficients are differences from the reference group `A`, adjusted for
the controls. The last lines of the summary report how much of the variation
of the probabilities the controls do not explain; this is the information the
estimate uses, discussed below.

`compare_hard()` shows what the most-likely-label regression would have
given on the same data.

```{r hard}
h <- compare_hard(fit)
h
```

```{r hard-numbers, include = FALSE}
est_hard <- h$estimates[h$estimates$method == "hard (cross-fitted)", ]
lim <- drop(h$distortion %*% attr(d, "tau"))
cov_hard <- h$coverage$coverage
f2 <- function(v) formatC(v, digits = 2, format = "f")
```

For group `B` the hard-label estimate is `r f2(est_hard$estimate[1])`, about
half of the true value of 1, and its interval excludes the true value. For
group `C` it is `r f2(est_hard$estimate[2])`, close to the true value of -0.5.
Replacing the probabilities by labels is a coarsening of the probabilities,
and with several groups its effect is a matrix: under the assumptions below,
the cross-fitted hard-label estimates converge to the distortion matrix times
the true effects, so the estimate for one group also picks up the effects of the
others through the off-diagonal entries. With the estimated matrix, the
limits are `r f2(lim[1])` for `B` and `r f2(lim[2])` for `C`. Both groups are
attenuated; for `C` the off-diagonal term moves the limit towards the true
value, and the estimate in this sample is closer still because of sampling
variation. Without the probabilities, neither the size nor the direction of
the hard-label error can be anticipated.

The last table translates the distortion into coverage. By an asymptotic
approximation, nominal 95% intervals around the cross-fitted hard-label
estimates would contain the true effect with probability of about
`r f2(cov_hard[1])` for `B` and `r f2(cov_hard[2])` for `C` in repeated
samples. The retention coefficients show that the distortion
is not the same along the two directions of the score information.

## What the method assumes

The estimand is \(\tau\) in

\[ E[Y \mid G, X] = \mu(X) + \sum_{k \ge 2} \tau_k \, 1\{G = k\}, \]

with \(\mu\) unrestricted, so \(\tau_k\) is the partial association between
group \(k\) (relative to the reference) and the outcome given the controls. It
is not a causal effect. Three conditions make it estimable from the
probabilities \(p\):

1. **Conditional calibration.** \(E[1\{G = k\} \mid p, X] = p_k\): among
   observations with the same probabilities and the same controls, the share
   in group \(k\) equals \(p_k\). This is stronger than the marginal
   calibration that Platt scaling or isotonic regression target.
2. **Information beyond the controls.** The classifier must use features that
   are not controls, so that no linear combination of the non-reference
   probabilities is a function of the controls. If the classifier used only
   the controls, the probabilities would be a function of the controls and the
   effect would not be identified.
3. **No direct effect of the extra features.** The classifier features that
   are not controls may affect the outcome only through the group.

Under these conditions, with \(a = p - E[p \mid X]\) and \(m(X) = E[Y \mid
X]\),

\[ E[a \, (Y - m(X))] = E[a a^\top] \, \tau , \]

and `soft_lm()` solves the sample version of this equation. The two nuisance
functions are estimated by cross-fitting, and the equation is
Neyman-orthogonal in both, so moderate errors in the nuisances do not bias the
estimate to first order. Standard errors are robust sandwich estimates.

The approach is related to regression calibration in the measurement-error
literature, which replaces an error-prone variable by its conditional
expectation. The difference is that the probabilities are first purged of the
controls; only the residual variation identifies the effect, and calibration
given the controls is what makes that residual variation informative.

## Choosing a learner

The nuisances \(E[Y \mid X]\) and \(E[p \mid X]\) are usually non-linear, and
the quality of the estimate depends on how well they are estimated. The
default learner is a random forest (`lrn_ranger()`). `lrn_lm()` fits
polynomials and is fast and deterministic; `lrn_glmnet()` fits a penalised
polynomial; `lrn_custom()` accepts any fitting and prediction functions.
Different learners can be used for the two nuisances.

```{r learners}
fit_rf <- soft_lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, probs = ~ prob_A + prob_B + prob_C,
                  data = d, learner = lrn_ranger(num.trees = 200),
                  n_rep = 5, seed = 1)
coef(fit_rf)

fit_mix <- update(fit, learner = list(m = lrn_ranger(num.trees = 200),
                                      r = lrn_lm(degree = 3)))
coef(fit_mix)
```

Repeating cross-fitting with new fold splits (`n_rep`) reduces the dependence
on a particular split; the reported variance then includes the spread across
splits. With random forests, five or more splits are advisable.

## Diagnostics

### Information beyond the controls

`score_spectrum()` decomposes \(E[a a^\top]\). For each direction it gives the
share of the variance of the probabilities that the controls do not explain. A
share close to zero means that the corresponding contrast is weakly
identified, and the eigenvector shows which groups it involves.

```{r spectrum}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Bar chart of the canonical shares of score variance not explained by
#|   the controls, one bar per direction.
score_spectrum(fit)
plot(fit, which = "spectrum")
```

### Checks on the labelled sample

Calibration and the absence of direct effects can be tested where the group
is observed. Here the flagged subsample plays that role.

```{r labelled}
lab <- d[d$labelled, ]
calibration_check(probs = ~ prob_A + prob_B + prob_C, group = "group",
                  data = lab, controls = ~ x1 + x2 + x3)
exclusion_test(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, group = "group", extra = ~ z, data = lab)
```

The calibration check reports a likelihood-ratio test of perfect calibration
and a test of calibration given the controls. The method needs calibration
given the controls, which the first test checks as a whole. The second test
isolates miscalibration that depends on the controls: if it rejects,
recalibrating the scores alone does not help, and they should be recalibrated
on the scores and the controls together, as `recalibrate()` does (see below).

### How much calibration error the conclusion tolerates

If the probabilities are miscalibrated by at most \(\delta\) in every
category, the bias of each coefficient is bounded by \(\delta\) times a factor
that `drift_sensitivity()` estimates. Its robustness values give the drift at
which the bound equals the estimate, and the drift at which the confidence
interval widened by the bound reaches zero.

```{r sensitivity}
drift_sensitivity(fit, delta = 0.02)
```

### All checks at once

`soft_check()` runs the checks and grades each as `ok`, `warning` or
`problem`.

```{r check}
soft_check(fit, labelled = lab, group = "group", extra = ~ z)
```

When something is wrong, the report says so. Below, the probabilities are
miscalibrated given the controls, and the classifier feature `z` affects the
outcome directly.

```{r check-bad}
bad <- sim_softcats(n = 6000, K = 2, miscalibration = 1.5,
                    direct_effect = 0.5, labelled_share = 0.4, seed = 2)
fit_bad <- soft_lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, probs = c("prob_A", "prob_B"),
                   data = bad, learner = lrn_lm(degree = 3), seed = 2)
soft_check(fit_bad, labelled = bad[bad$labelled, ], group = "group",
           extra = ~ z)
```

### Recalibration

When calibration fails, the labelled sample can also repair it.
`recalibrate()` fits a multinomial logit of the observed group on the
log-odds of the probabilities, the controls and their products. It checks the
recalibrated probabilities on folds of the labelled sample that were not used
to fit the map, and recomputes the estimate with the folds of the fit.

Recalibration needs enough labelled observations for the map, so we simulate
a larger sample, with three groups as in the first example. Doubling the
log-odds of its probabilities makes them overconfident.

```{r recalibrate}
o <- sim_softcats(n = 4000, K = 3, seed = 1)
P <- as.matrix(o[, c("prob_A", "prob_B", "prob_C")])
o[, c("over_A", "over_B", "over_C")] <- P^2 / rowSums(P^2)
fit_over <- soft_lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, probs = c("over_A", "over_B", "over_C"),
                    data = o, learner = lrn_lm(degree = 3), seed = 1)
rc <- recalibrate(fit_over, labelled = o[o$labelled, ], group = "group")
rc
```

```{r recalibrate-numbers, include = FALSE}
re <- rc$estimates
```

The overconfident probabilities attenuate the effect of `B` to
`r f2(re$estimate[1])`. They fail the overall calibration test but not the
test of calibration given the controls, because the miscalibration does not
depend on the controls. The recalibrated probabilities pass both tests out of
fold, and the estimates, `r f2(re$estimate[3])` and `r f2(re$estimate[4])`,
are close to the true values of 1 and -0.5. `predict()` recalibrates the
probabilities of any data set, for example to refit the model with other
options.

```{r recalibrate-predict}
o[, c("rec_A", "rec_B", "rec_C")] <- predict(rc, o)
coef(update(fit_over, probs = c("rec_A", "rec_B", "rec_C")))
```

Recalibration repairs calibration, not a direct effect of the classifier
features. In the example with both failures, the recalibrated probabilities
pass the calibration check, but the estimate stays far from the true value
of 1. A map that pulls the probabilities towards their mean given the
controls can even amplify such a bias, so `recalibrate()` also reports the
information beyond the controls before and after recalibration.

```{r recalibrate-bad}
rc_bad <- recalibrate(fit_bad, labelled = bad[bad$labelled, ],
                      group = "group")
rc_bad$estimates
```

The standard errors after recalibration treat the map as known. They do not
include its estimation error and can be too small when the labelled sample is
small compared with the estimation sample.

## Two groups and confidence thresholds

With two groups, `kappa_curve()` shows the attenuation factor of the label
\(1\{p > t\}\) across thresholds \(t\). Values far below one mean that
thresholding at \(t\) discards much of the signal.

```{r kappa}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Line chart of the attenuation factor kappa against the confidence
#|   threshold, with a dashed line at one for no attenuation.
b <- sim_softcats(n = 3000, K = 2, seed = 3)
fit_b <- soft_lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, probs = b$prob_B, data = b,
                 learner = lrn_lm(degree = 3), seed = 3)
kc <- kappa_curve(fit_b, thresholds = seq(0.5, 0.9, by = 0.1))
kc[, c("threshold", "share_positive", "kappa", "estimate_hard",
       "estimate_soft")]
plot(kc)
```

## Weights and clusters

Survey weights and clustered designs are supported. With `cluster`, standard
errors are cluster-robust and the cross-fitting folds are formed from whole
clusters.

```{r design}
set.seed(1)
d$w <- runif(nrow(d), 0.5, 2)
d$area <- rep(seq_len(300), each = 10)
fit_w <- soft_lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, probs = ~ prob_A + prob_B + prob_C,
                 data = d, weights = ~ w, cluster = ~ area,
                 learner = lrn_lm(degree = 3), seed = 1)
summary(fit_w)$coefficients
```

## Working with other packages

Fits support the usual model methods (`coef()`, `vcov()`, `confint()`,
`nobs()`, `update()`), and `tidy()` and `glance()` for broom. They therefore
work in tables produced by modelsummary and with `lmtest::coeftest()`.

```{r compat}
tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
glance(fit)
```

```{r compat-other, eval = requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE)}
lmtest::coeftest(fit)
```
